strengths: Careful and extensive empirical evaluation: the authors retrain baselines (Pairformer and a sequence-only Transformer) across three model sizes and compare at matched training budgets rather than only reporting end-of-training checkpoints, which makes the efficiency–accuracy tradeoff claims credible.

The core finding—that triangle attention and sequence updates in the Pairformer can be removed without sacrificing accuracy while cutting training cost by ~34% and achieving up to 4x faster inference on long sequences—is valuable and well-supported (Figure 1, Figure 4, Tables 4-5), with potential practical impact on downstream use cases like binder design (BindFast, Table 1) and large-complex modeling.

The evaluation spans multiple relevant settings (protein folding, protein-protein and protein-ligand docking on RCSB and CASP15) against state-of-the-art systems (AF3, Chai-1, Boltz-1), with oracle and top-1 reporting and confidence intervals.

The analysis section adds scientific insight beyond raw numbers: the low-norm dropout experiment showing triangle multiplication encodes sparse interactions, and the Match3 probe separating the role of quadratic pair representations from cubic compute are both interesting and reasonably designed.
Comprehensive hyperparameter tables (Table 6) and FLOPs analysis (Table 2, Appendix B) support reproducibility of the training setup.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The architecture is essentially an ablation of the Pairformer: removing triangle attention and sequence updates while keeping triangle multiplication (which is itself established in AlphaFold2, Genie2, MiniFold, MSA Pairformer). The contribution is an empirical demonstration rather than a new mechanism or theoretical insight, which limits the paper's intellectual depth.

Accuracy is not fully matched to state of the art: Pairmixer lags Boltz-1 on DockQ>0.23 (0.63 vs 0.64 oracle) and its large model does not reach the public Boltz-1 checkpoint (Table 4), so the claim of 'matching state-of-the-art' is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

Comparisons to external systems are partly compromised: results for AF3/Chai-1 are taken from the literature rather than re-evaluated, and Pairmixer lacks a confidence head, so top-1 comparisons against systems with confidence ranking are inherently unfavorable/unfair and should be discussed more carefully.

The Transformer baseline required architectural modifications (outer-sum pair features from sequence, modified MSA-to-diffusion connections), which weakens it as a controlled comparison and makes attribution of the pair-representation benefit less clean.

Several presentation and consistency issues undermine polish: Section 5.3 cites 'Figure 4' when the runtime analysis is in Figure 5; the Figure 12 caption refers to 'the Transformer architecture' when comparing against Boltz-1/Pairformer; typos ('structrually', 'realizes', 'BotlzDesign'); and CASP15 results appear in Figure 11 but are referenced as 'Table 11', which is never clearly defined.

The BindFast downstream comparison is mostly runtime/qualitative; quantitative design success rates or validation metrics for the designed binders are missing, so the design claims rest largely on speed rather than demonstrated design quality.

The low-norm dropout analysis is post-hoc (applied at inference to a model trained without dropout), so the conclusion that 'triangle multiplication identifies essential sparse interactions' is suggestive but not fully established; no retraining with sparsification is reported.

strengths: The paper performs a well-controlled architectural study: the Pairmixer, Pairformer, and Transformer backbones are trained with identical data, schedules, and diffusion modules across small/medium/large scales, which makes the efficiency/accuracy trade-off claims credible.

Extensive empirical evaluation: RCSB and CASP15 test sets, multiple metrics (lDDT, DockQ, lDDT-PLI, RMSD), inference-time profiling across token counts/recycles/MSA depths, FLOPs breakdowns, and ablations over FFN and triangle-multiplication dimensions and alternative mixers (Table 3).

Concrete demonstration of practical value in a downstream application: BindFast (Pairmixer inside BoltzDesign) achieves 2-2.6x sampling speedups and extends the feasible target size from ~500 to ~650 residues before OOM, which is a tangible benefit for hallucination-based design loops.

The Match3 analysis (Section 6/C.5) is a nice touch that isolates the representational capacity of triangle multiplication from sequence-length effects and connects the empirical results to a theoretical benchmark.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is removing two modules (triangle attention and sequence updates) from an existing architecture (Pairformer/Boltz-1). Attention-free and triangle-multiplication-only backbones have already been explored (Minifold, Genie2, MSA Pairformer, IgFold), and the paper itself acknowledges this. The method amounts to an incremental ablation-style simplification of a public model rather than a new architectural idea.

The headline claim of 'matching state-of-the-art' is stronger than the evidence. On CASP15 (Table 5), Pairformer outperforms Pairmixer on most metrics (e.g., lDDT 0.42 vs 0.41, DockQ 0.64 vs 0.52, RMSD<2 0.28 vs 0.31 at large scale), and on RCSB Pairmixer lags on DockQ (0.63 vs 0.64) and DockQ>0.49. The paper's own head-to-head figure (Figure 12) shows Pairmixer wins less than 50% of the time on most metrics versus its own baseline. 'Comparable' would be accurate; 'matching SOTA predictors such as AlphaFold and Chai-1' overstates the result.

The system-level comparison in Figure 6 is not apples-to-apples: the authors do not train a confidence head, so their 'top-1' numbers are simply the first sampled pose, while AF3/Chai-1/Boltz-1 top-1 numbers use learned confidence ranking. Combined with oracle reporting, this weakens the central competitiveness claim and muddies the practical comparison.

Docking performance, arguably where pair representations and triangle reasoning should matter most for complexes, degrades the most (DockQ and interface metrics), which somewhat contradicts the narrative that triangle attention is 'unnecessary' and that Pairmixer 'preserves higher-order geometric reasoning'. The paper does not adequately explain or investigate this regression.

Efficiency claims are partly diluted: the retained triangle multiplication still scales cubically in L, so the approach does not change asymptotic complexity, only constants; the paper could be clearer that the speedup is implementation/constant-factor rather than a complexity improvement.

No code or model release is mentioned, and given the results hinge on reproducing Boltz-1 training at ~200-400 GPU-days per run plus finetuning, reproducibility is a significant concern. Missing details on hyperparameter selection for the modified Transformer baseline (an architecture the authors themselves designed and tuned) also raises the possibility of a comparatively weak non-Pairformer control.

The evaluation is limited to relatively short training schedules (53k + 15k iterations) and modest model sizes; it remains open whether the Pairmixer-vs-Pairformer parity holds at the scale and training budget of production models (e.g., Boltz-2, AF3), especially since the accuracy gap between the two backbones is small but consistently favors Pairformer.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck: the cubic scaling of triangle attention in AlphaFold3-style cofolding backbones, which directly limits high-throughput screening, proteome-scale folding, and hallucination-based design.

The core simplification (retaining triangle multiplication + FFNs, removing triangle attention and sequence updates) is well motivated and empirically validated: Pairmixer matches or exceeds Pairformer at small/medium scales and matches it at large scale (0.78 mean lDDT) with ~34% less training compute and up to 4x faster inference at 2048 tokens.

Evaluation is unusually extensive for this area: three model sizes, equal-training-budget comparisons, RCSB and CASP15 test sets, FLOPs analysis, ablations (mixing method, dimensions, diffusion depth), and a downstream application (BindFast in BoltzDesign) demonstrating 2-2.6x speedups and OOM-free generation on targets beyond 650 residues.

The analysis sections are thoughtful: the low-norm dropout experiment showing triangle multiplication encodes sparse triplet interactions, and the Match3 study isolating the role of pair representations vs. compute order, add scientific insight beyond a pure engineering result.
Honest framing of several comparisons (e.g., Pairmixer lags on DockQ>0.23, Transformer is fastest overall) increases credibility of the reported results.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: removing triangle attention from AlphaFold-style backbones to rely on triangle multiplication has been explored (Minifold/MiniFold, Genie2, MSA Pairformer), and the paper's distinguishing claim (first such simplification for AF3-like cofolding) is an application/context-level contribution rather than a new architectural primitive or theoretical insight.

The headline accuracy comparison is not fully fair: Pairmixer has no confidence head, so its 'top-1' uses the first prediction while AF3/Chai-1/Boltz-1 use trained confidence models for ranking. Oracle results partially mitigate this, but practical system-level comparisons are confounded, and the paper understates this gap.

Head-to-head win rates against the retrained Pairformer (Figure 12) are below 50% on lDDT (44.9%), RMSD (45.8%), and lDDT-PLI (40.0%); the narrative of 'matching' Pairformer is somewhat stronger than the per-complex evidence, even if aggregate metrics are close.

Ligand/protein-protein results on CASP15 are thin (n=13-14 complexes), and DockQ>0.23 lags the Pairformer notably (0.52 vs 0.64 at large scale), suggesting possible weaknesses in interface modeling that are not deeply analyzed.

A few presentation inconsistencies: Section 5.3 says 'In Figure 4' when referring to inference benchmarks (should be Figure 5); Figure 12's caption copy-pastes the Transformer comparison text; BindFast quality is evaluated only qualitatively (Figure 13), with no quantitative design success-rate comparison to BoltzDesign.
No statement about code/model release is evident, which limits reproducibility for a systems-efficiency paper whose value lies in community adoption.
Some efficiency claims mix hardware settings (GH200 for inference benchmarks, A100 for BindFast, H200 for training), making direct comparisons across tables harder to interpret.

strengths: Clear and practically motivated contribution: showing that triangle attention and sequence updates can be removed from the Pairformer while retaining triangle multiplication is a simple but consequential architectural finding for cofolding models

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple model sizes (small/medium/large), matched training FLOPs and GPU-days, RCSB and CASP15 test sets, plus diverse benchmarks (PoseBusters, antibody-antigen, protein-nucleic acid, RNA)

Strong efficiency results with concrete numbers: up to 4x inference speedup at 2048 tokens, ~34% training cost reduction, and demonstrated downstream utility in BindFast (2x+ speedups, larger designable targets)

Thorough analysis section: head-to-head win rates vs. both Transformer and Pairformer, distogram evaluation isolating backbone quality, recycling sensitivity, stratification by MSA depth and sequence length, and sparse-interaction probing via low-norm and blockwise dropout

Useful ablations (Table 6, Table 7) isolating contributions of sequence updates, triangle attention, triangle multiplication, FFN dimensions, and alternative mixers; the Match3 task analysis (D.3) nicely separates representational from computational effects
Reproducibility appears strong: hyperparameters, FLOPs accounting, training schedules, and code availability are documented
weaknesses: Accuracy claims are slightly stronger than the evidence: at the largest scale Pairmixer slightly trails the Pairformer baseline (lDDT 0.78 vs. Boltz-1 public 0.79; DockQ>0.23 0.63 vs. 0.64; RMSD<2 0.55 vs. 0.57 in Table 4 Phase 2), and 'matches state-of-the-art' is only supported at parity-within-noise rather than clear equivalence

Main comparisons use oracle-over-5-poses evaluation, and Pairmixer lacks a confidence model so 'top-1' comparisons vs. AF3/Chai-1/Boltz-1 (which have confidence models) are not apples-to-apples; this weakens the system-level SOTA claims

Novelty is incremental: triangle-multiplication-only backbones exist in prior work (MiniFold's Miniformer, Genie2, MSA Pairformer); the contribution is extending this finding to AlphaFold3-style cofolding rather than a fundamentally new mechanism

The Pairformer ablation (Table 6) shows removing triangle attention degrades performance (lDDT 0.70 vs 0.74) under the standard schedule, so the 'attention is unnecessary' conclusion depends on extended training; the compute-optimal-equivalence framing could be stated more carefully
Small test sets for several benchmarks (RNA n=27, antibody-antigen n=70) and no statistical significance testing for the central parity claims, though bootstrapped CIs appear in figures

Efficiency gains are architecture-inherent but partially offset by still-cubic triangle multiplication; the paper does not explore sub-cubic alternatives or compare against other efficiency techniques (e.g., Strassen attention, sparsity), limiting the sense of a fully explored design space

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple model sizes (small/medium/large), RCSB and CASP15 test sets, and diverse biomolecular benchmarks (PoseBusters, antibody-antigen, protein-nucleic acid, RNA), which is more thorough than typical architecture-simplification papers.

Clear efficiency gains are demonstrated concretely: up to 4x faster inference at 2048 tokens, ~2x faster sampling in BoltzDesign, and extension to sequences beyond Pairformer's memory limit (~700 amino acids).

Useful analysis sections: distogram-based isolation of backbone contribution, recycling sensitivity checks, sparse-interaction probing via low-norm and blockwise dropout, and a Match3 synthetic task separating pair-representation benefits from cubic compute.
Ablation tables (Table 6, Table 7) covering each removed Pairformer module, hidden-dimension sensitivities, and alternative mixing functions (FFT, pooling) strengthen the empirical story.
Built on the reproducible Boltz-1 codebase with hyperparameters and FLOPs accounting provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is an ablation-style removal of existing components (triangle attention and sequence updates) from an established architecture. Prior work (MiniFold, SimpleFold, MSA Pairformer, Genie2) already showed triangle multiplication or lighter backbones suffice; the contribution is applying this known simplification to the AF3-style cofolding setting, which is more engineering than new insight.

Central claims of 'matching state-of-the-art' are overstated. On CASP15 (Table 5, Figure 12), Pairmixer clearly lags Pairformer on protein-protein assembly (DockQ>0.23: 0.49-0.52 vs 0.64-0.68 across scales), and the public Boltz-1 checkpoint outperforms retrained versions on nearly every metric (e.g., lDDT 0.79 vs 0.78; RMSD<2: 0.57 vs 0.55). The abstract's parity claim is not consistently supported.
No confidence model is trained, so top-1 comparisons (the practically relevant setting for downstream users) are missing or unfavorable, weakening the deployment-relevance argument.

Multiple confounded changes at once: triangle attention is removed from both the backbone and the MSA module simultaneously, and the Transformer baseline requires an altered MSA-module/diffusion wiring (A.2), making clean attribution of improvements harder.

Cubic scaling is retained: triangle multiplication is still O(L^3), so the paper does not actually address the asymptotic bottleneck it motivates the paper with; gains are constant-factor, and the memory-extension results are the only true scaling win.

Comparison of Fig. 6 numbers to literature values for AF3/Chai-1 without identical evaluation protocols raises fairness concerns; the oracle-vs-top-1 asymmetry with respect to prior work (which has confidence models) is not adequately controlled.

Some evidence is mixed or under-explained: the Transformer baseline beats both pair-based models on RNA (Table 1d), which is waved off as data scarcity; win rates against Pairformer hover around 40-45% (Fig. 15), i.e., essentially parity rather than an advantage.

Writing/overclaiming issues: the title 'Triangle Multiplication is All You Need' is not supported (the Pairformer ablation in Table 6 shows removing either triangular module alone degrades performance at short training, contradicting the 'all you need' framing); 'training in 34% fewer GPU-days' claims vary across sections (34% vs 1.5x).

strengths: The central finding — that triangle attention and sequence updates can be removed from the Pairformer while retaining triangle multiplication and FFNs, with no loss in accuracy — is a clean, well-motivated architectural simplification with direct practical value for large-scale cofolding applications.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: three model sizes, controlled equal-iteration and equal-GPU-day training comparisons, the Boltz-1 RCSB test set, CASP15, PoseBusters, antibody-antigen, protein-nucleic acid, and RNA benchmarks, all against well-known strong baselines (AF3, Chai-1, Boltz-1).

Extensive ablations strengthen the paper: module-by-module Pairformer ablations (Table 6), mixing-method ablations (FFT, AvgPool vs. TriMul), diffusion-depth sensitivity, distogram/contact prediction to isolate backbone quality, and recycling-step sensitivity analysis.

The paper goes beyond prediction and demonstrates the practical payoff in a downstream application (BindFast / BoltzDesign), showing 2-2.6x speedups and extending feasible target sizes by ~30% before OOM — concrete evidence that the efficiency gains translate to real workflows.

The analysis section is insightful: the low-norm vs. random dropout experiments (Figures 8-9) provide a genuinely interesting observation that triangle multiplication concentrates its computation on a sparse subset of long-range interactions, and the Match3 task (Section D.3) cleanly separates the contribution of quadratic pair representations from cubic compute.
Code is released, and the implementation on top of Boltz-1 with public checkpoints and reported GPU-days/FLOPs (Table 10) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core observation builds on prior work showing triangle-multiplication-only backbones suffice (MiniFold/Miniformer for Evoformer, Genie2, MSA Pairformer). The contribution is a transfer and validation of this idea to AlphaFold3-style cofolding models rather than a new architectural mechanism; the title's 'is all you need' framing overstates this.

Evaluation relies on oracle (best-of-5) predictions because no confidence head is trained, while all baselines report both oracle and top-1. The 'top-1*' numbers use the first prediction without a confidence model, making system-level comparisons to AF3/Chai-1/Boltz-1 less like-for-like; the field typically uses confidence-ranked top-1 results.

Results are 'matching' but mostly slightly below the Pairformer baseline at equal training (e.g., CASP15 DockQ 0.52 vs 0.64, lDDT 0.41 vs 0.42, and the Boltz-1 public checkpoint at 0.79 lDDT vs 0.78), so the headline 'matches state-of-the-art' claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence; the efficiency-vs-accuracy trade-off should be presented more carefully.

Some writing/presentation errors undermine polish: Section 5.3 says 'In Figure 4' when Figure 5 is meant; Figure 15's caption describes comparing to the Transformer but the axes compare to Boltz-1; the Table 4/Table 5 vs. Figure 12 discrepancy in CASP15 numbers is only briefly explained; and several claims (e.g., 'consistently outperforms or matches') conflict with specific table entries.

The Transformer baseline being the strongest on RNA-only structures (Table 1d) is noted but not investigated; with n=27 this raises questions about statistical power across the smaller benchmarks (DockQ n=13-14 on CASP15).

Only single runs per configuration appear to be reported; given the tight margins (0.01-0.02 lDDT differences in places), variance across seeds is not quantified, although error bars are shown on the system-level plots.

The abstract's claim of '34% training cost reduction' is derived from GPU-days at matched accuracy, which depends on curve-fitting of the training-time plots; a clearer accounting (FLOPs in Table 10 suggests ~1.7x fewer FLOPs, not 3x) would help align the efficiency claims.
